newsitem.title: USA: Bulge seen in bull semen exports to Mexico - attache.
newsitem.headline: Bulge seen in bull semen exports to Mexico - attache.

text.p: Mexico is an important market for U.S. breeding cattle and genetic products despite a decline in imports during 1995, a U.S. agricultural attache said in a report released Thursday.
The report, prepared by the U.S. Embassy in Mexico City, said Mexico's imports from the U.S. should rebound "despite deep cuts in imports during 1995."

Mexican imports of breeding cattle in 1994 were more than $32 million but shrank 69 pct to $10.3 million in 1995. The 1996 figures show "significant improvement," recording $7.7 million for the first semester, the report said.
"Import demand for many products is expected to remain strong in the long term," the report stated.

The strongest competition the United States faces is from Canada, which traditionally holds more dollar market share than percentage of volume. This is explained by the superior stock Canadian cattle is considered to have, the report said.

In 1994, Mexico was the top international customer for breeding stock for the United States, accounting for about 75 percent of all U.S. shipments. Bull semen exports to Mexico that year were about nine percent of all U.S. exports.

U.S. exports of breeding stock grew strongly until 1991 when they reached $60 million. All categories, especially beef, declined sharply for the next two years, reaching a low of $34 million in 1993, due partly to a drought in northern Mexico.
In 1994, however, U.S. exports rebounded 70 pct to $61.3 million, but the devaluation brought imports to a low of $21.9 million in 1995.

Although bull semen exports were down from $4.2 million in 1992 to $3.8 million in 1994, the report said, "there is a strong positive trend." Unlike other categories, bull semen imports from the United States only suffered an 8 percent decline.
